items.section_heading: TWO MARKS QUESTIONS | Board 2024 OD Standard
items.stem: Prove that 5 − 2√3 is an irrational number. It is given that √3 is an irrational number.
items.answer: Assume that 5 − 2√3 is a rational number. Then it can be written as p/q where p and q are co-prime integers and q ≠ 0, so 5 − 2√3 = p/q. Rewriting, 2√3 = 5 − p/q, i.e. √3 = (5q − p)/(2q). Here (5q − p)/(2q) is rational because p and q are co-prime integers, so √3 would have to be a rational number. But √3 is irrational. This contradicts the given fact. Hence 5 − 2√3 is an irrational number.

items.section_heading: TWO MARKS QUESTIONS | Board 2024 OD Standard
items.stem: Show that the number 5 × 11 × 17 + 3 × 11 is a composite number.
items.answer: 5 × 11 × 17 + 3 × 11 = 11(5 × 17 + 3) = 11 × (85 + 3) = 11 × 88 = 11 × 8 × 11 = 2³ × 11². Since 5 × 11 × 17 + 3 × 11 can be factorised as 2³ × 11², it has factors other than 1 and itself. Thus it is a composite number.

items.section_heading: TWO MARKS QUESTIONS | Board 2023 OD Standard
items.stem: Show that 6ⁿ cannot end with digit 0 for any natural number n.
items.answer: If the number 6ⁿ, for any n, were to end with the digit zero, then it would be divisible by 5, i.e. the prime factorisation of 6ⁿ would contain the prime 5. This is not possible because the only primes in the factorisation of 6ⁿ = (2 × 3)ⁿ are 2 and 3. The uniqueness of the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic guarantees that there are no other primes in the factorisation of 6ⁿ. Since there is no prime factor 5, 6ⁿ cannot end with the digit zero.

items.section_heading: TWO MARKS QUESTIONS | Board 2023 OD Standard
items.stem: Find the HCF and LCM of 72 and 120.
items.answer: By prime factorisation, 72 = 2³ × 3² and 120 = 2³ × 3¹ × 5¹. HCF(72, 120) = 2³ × 3¹ = 8 × 3 = 24. LCM(72, 120) = 2³ × 3² × 5 = 8 × 9 × 5 = 360. Thus the HCF and LCM of 72 and 120 are 24 and 360 respectively.

items.section_heading: TWO MARKS QUESTIONS | Board Term-1 2012
items.stem: Explain why (7 × 13 × 11) + 11 and (7 × 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1) + 3 are composite numbers.
items.answer: (7 × 13 × 11) + 11 = 11 × (7 × 13 + 1) = 11 × (91 + 1) = 11 × 92. And (7 × 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1) + 3 = 3(7 × 6 × 5 × 4 × 2 × 1 + 1) = 3 × 1681 = 3 × 41 × 41. Since the given numbers have more than two prime factors, both numbers are composite.

items.section_heading: TWO MARKS QUESTIONS | Board Term-1 2017
items.stem: Explain whether 3 × 12 × 101 + 4 is a prime number or a composite number.
items.answer: A prime number is a natural number greater than 1 that cannot be formed by multiplying two smaller natural numbers; a natural number greater than 1 that is not prime is called a composite number. Every composite number can be written as the product of two or more (not necessarily distinct) primes. Here 3 × 12 × 101 + 4 = 4(3 × 3 × 101 + 1) = 4(909 + 1) = 4(910) = 2 × 2 × (10 × 7 × 13) = 2 × 2 × 2 × 5 × 7 × 13, which is a composite number.

items.section_heading: TWO MARKS QUESTIONS | Board Term-1 2013
items.stem: Given that HCF (306, 1314) = 18. Find LCM (306, 1314).
items.answer: Let a = 306 and b = 1314. We know LCM(a, b) × HCF(a, b) = a × b. Substituting, LCM(a, b) × 18 = 306 × 1314, so LCM(a, b) = (306 × 1314)/18. Thus LCM(306, 1314) = 22,338.

items.section_heading: TWO MARKS QUESTIONS | Board Term-1 2015
items.stem: Check whether 4ⁿ can end with the digit 0 for any natural number n.
items.answer: If the number 4ⁿ, for any n, were to end with the digit zero, then it would be divisible by 5 and 2, i.e. the prime factorisation of 4ⁿ would contain the primes 5 and 2. This is not possible because the only prime in the factorisation of 4ⁿ = 2²ⁿ is 2. The uniqueness of the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic guarantees that there are no other primes in the factorisation of 4ⁿ. So there is no natural number n for which 4ⁿ ends with the digit zero. Hence 4ⁿ cannot end with the digit zero.

items.section_heading: TWO MARKS QUESTIONS | Board Term-1 2015
items.stem: Show that 5√6 is an irrational number.
items.answer: Let 5√6 be a rational number, which can be expressed as a/b where b ≠ 0 and a, b are co-prime. Then 5√6 = a/b, so √6 = a/(5b), i.e. √6 = rational. But √6 is an irrational number. Thus our assumption is wrong. Hence 5√6 is an irrational number.

items.section_heading: TWO MARKS QUESTIONS | Board Term-1 2013
items.stem: Write a rational number between √2 and √3.
items.answer: We need a rational number x such that (1/10)√200 < x < (1/10)√300. Choosing any perfect square such as 225 or 256 lying between 200 and 300: x = √(225/100) = 15/10 = 3/2. Similarly, choosing 256, x = √(256/100) = 16/10 = 8/5. So 3/2 (or 8/5) is a rational number between √2 and √3.

items.section_heading: TWO MARKS QUESTIONS
items.stem: Show that 571 is a prime number.
items.answer: Let x = 571, so √x = √571. Now 571 lies between the perfect squares (23)² = 529 and (24)² = 576. The prime numbers less than 24 are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19 and 23. Since 571 is not divisible by any of these numbers, 571 is a prime number.

items.section_heading: TWO MARKS QUESTIONS | Sample Paper 2017
items.stem: If two positive integers p and q are written as p = a²b³ and q = a³b, where a and b are prime numbers, then verify LCM(p, q) × HCF(p, q) = pq.
items.answer: We have p = a²b³ = a × a × b × b × b and q = a³b = a × a × a × b. Now LCM(p, q) = a × a × a × b × b × b = a³b³ and HCF(p, q) = a × a × b = a²b. Therefore LCM(p, q) × HCF(p, q) = a³b³ × a²b = a⁵b⁴ = a²b³ × a³b = pq. Hence verified.

items.section_heading: TWO MARKS QUESTIONS | Board 2010
items.stem: Prove that 3 + √5 is an irrational number.
items.answer: Assume that 3 + √5 is a rational number. Then 3 + √5 = p/q with q ≠ 0, so √5 = p/q − 3 = (p − 3q)/q. Here √5 is irrational while (p − 3q)/q is rational, and a rational number cannot be equal to an irrational number. Hence 3 + √5 is an irrational number.

items.section_heading: TWO MARKS QUESTIONS | Board Term-1 2016
items.stem: Show that any positive even integer can be written in the form 6q, 6q + 2 or 6q + 4, where q is an integer.
items.answer: Let a be any positive integer. By Euclid's division algorithm a can be written as a = bq + r. Take b = 6; then 0 ≤ r < 6 because 0 ≤ r < b. Thus a = 6q, 6q + 1, 6q + 2, 6q + 3, 6q + 4 or 6q + 5. Here 6q, 6q + 2 and 6q + 4 are divisible by 2, so they are even positive integers. Hence a is always an even integer if a = 6q, 6q + 2 or 6q + 4.

items.section_heading: TWO MARKS QUESTIONS | Board 2019, 2017 | PRACTICE
items.stem: Show that any positive odd integer is of the form 4q + 1 or 4q + 3, where q is some integer.
items.answer: By Euclid's division algorithm, a = 4q + r with 0 ≤ r < 4, so a = 4q, 4q + 1, 4q + 2 or 4q + 3. Of these 4q and 4q + 2 are divisible by 2 and hence even, so every positive odd integer is of the form 4q + 1 or 4q + 3.
